job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Olga Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my dad in Corby Row, in the house where I grew up. He drives a city bus and is out by five, so I get up with him and make his lunch. Then I sit at the desk in my old bedroom and go through the engineering job boards, one by one, the way I was taught: read the advert, write a proper letter, send it. After lunch I walk to the library to use the printer and read trade magazines. Some days I help my neighbour Mrs Harlan with her shopping because it gets me outside.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How have the months since graduating been?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Long. I did mechanical engineering and finished in June with a good grade. My final project was a test rig for a gearbox, and I did a ten-week internship at a pump factory in the next town. I like the workshop side, drawing a part and then holding it. Since June I've sent about seventy applications, had two interviews and no offers. I owe a big student loan, my savings are almost nothing, and Dad can't help, he's already stretched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, finally some sense. AI saving a bit of time here and there is fine. I'd tell my friends from uni that the sensible thing is to carry on and not panic, and I'd say the real problem is that companies don't give graduates a proper first job any more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means the same slow market. Mechanical jobs near us are few, and the pump factory told me they won't hire this year. A plateau doesn't make me safer or more worried than I am now. I'd still be sending letters into a void, with the loan statements arriving every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep sending applications but spread them wider, to maintenance technician and quality inspector roles as well as design. I'd ask the pump factory's engineer, Mr Lindqvist, to keep me in mind. I'd take a part-time workshop job if one came up, even at low pay, and I'd keep helping at home so Dad doesn't pay for everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Flat. Not terrible, not good, just heavy. Like carrying a bag of shopping up four floors with no lift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a plateau do to the pump factory and firms like it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the pump factory gives me a call, I'd go back tomorrow. If they don't, I'd try the maintenance side of other factories. I'd also ask the local college whether they need a workshop assistant. The point is to get a foot inside any place with machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you change about how you're searching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending the whole morning on one letter. I've been polishing each one, and maybe it's better to send twice as many and keep them shorter. A friend told me that, and I resisted it. I like doing things properly, but doing things properly hasn't gotten me an offer.

say: I'd tell friends to carry on and not panic, because AI saving some time changes **little**.
The real problem is that firms give graduates no proper first job.
think: A plateau means the same slow market, with **loan** statements arriving every month.
The pump factory won't hire this year, and few mechanical jobs are nearby.
do: Apply wider to maintenance technician and quality **inspector** roles as well as design.
Ask Mr Lindqvist at the pump factory to keep me in mind.
Take any part-time workshop job, even at low pay.
feel: **Flat** and heavy, like carrying shopping up four floors with no lift.
S0.quote: I like doing things properly, but doing things properly hasn't gotten me an offer.
fieldNote: She is **methodical**, and she is only now loosening her habit of polishing each application.
Her father cannot help, so she carries the loan and the household chores at once.
She prefers workshop work and sees the **hands-on** side as her way in.

steps.text: Apply for maintenance technician and quality inspector jobs
Ask Mr Lindqvist at the pump factory to keep her in mind
Send shorter letters to twice as many firms
Ask the local college about a workshop assistant job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's something that firms and the government need to handle carefully. We shouldn't rush to ban it or to cheer for it. I'd say that jobs for beginners should be protected somehow, because if software does the starter tasks, nobody learns the trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it worries me more than I admit. The starter tasks in mechanical engineering are drawings, parts lists, checking tolerances and writing test reports. At the pump factory I did most of that. If software does those, there's no step for people like me to stand on. I'm not as exposed as someone in office work, but I'm closer to the edge than I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look harder at jobs where the work is on the shop floor, like maintenance, commissioning and testing. I'd also finally try one of these AI tools, but only for small things like checking my letters. I wouldn't hand it my drawings. I'd ask Dad's friend at the bus depot, a mechanic, whether there's work, since buses need engineers too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Edgy. I don't like the idea of learning something new just because I'm pushed, but I can see I won't have much choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of the pump factory's engineering work would software take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The drawing and the paperwork. The stuff where you take a standard part and check it against a standard. Software is good at that, you give it the numbers and it gives you the answer. Software can't stand on a factory floor and hear that a bearing sounds wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start using AI tools in that case?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I suppose, yes, in the end. I've never used one, and I'm not proud of that. I'm wary of putting my work into something that I don't understand. But if all the firms are using it, then refusing is like refusing to learn the computer in the nineties. I'd start small and see.

say: I'd say we shouldn't rush to ban AI or cheer for it, but **beginner** jobs need protecting.
If software does starter tasks, nobody learns the trade.
think: The starter tasks I did at the pump factory are the ones software does, so there's no **step** to stand on.
I'm closer to the edge than I'd like.
do: Look at **shop-floor** jobs like maintenance, commissioning and testing.
Try an AI tool for small things, such as checking my letters.
Ask Dad's friend, a mechanic at the bus depot, whether there's work.
feel: **Edgy**, because I don't like learning something just because I'm pushed.
I can see I won't have much choice.
S1.quote: Software can't stand on a factory floor and hear that a bearing sounds wrong.
fieldNote: She is **wary** of AI mainly because she does not understand it, not because of principle.
The bus depot link shows how she uses family contacts for trade jobs.
Her plan is to start **small**, with letters, and keep drawings to herself.

steps.text: Apply for factory maintenance and commissioning jobs
Try an AI tool for checking application letters only
Ask Dad's mechanic friend about work at the bus depot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and governments and firms have to slow down and look after people. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen, probably in a letter to the council and the MP, because I'm not someone who shouts online. Plans and help should be ready before it lands, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm scared. Two years isn't enough. I'd barely have a first job, and then the thinking side of mechanical work goes, the drawings, the design, the planning. And with no savings and a loan, I'm close to the edge. I don't see a place where someone like me fits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first job I could get, even something low, and I'd ask Dad if I can stay at home as long as possible. I'd stop sending letters for design roles and go for workshop and maintenance jobs, because robots in the workshop come later. I'd also visit the job centre, which I haven't done yet because I was embarrassed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cold. I'd feel dizzy when I think about it. It's like being told the bridge you're walking on will be closed before you get across.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your dad that evening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cook his favourite meal, sit him down and tell him the whole thing. I'd say I need to stay a bit longer, and I'm sorry. He'd say it's your home, you're not a burden, but I'd see him worry about the bills. My dad is sixty and I don't want him driving buses forever because of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does knowing robots come three years later help you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. About three years extra for the hands-on side is something to hold on to. If I get a job on the floor, I might have until 2031 before robots really arrive. But it's thin comfort when the planning and ordering parts of that job get taken first.

say: I'd write to the council and my MP, because plans and **help** should be ready before this lands.
I don't shout online, but I'd say it too fast.
think: Two years isn't enough, and thinking work like drawings and design goes **first**.
With a loan and no savings, I don't see where someone like me fits.
do: Take the first job I can get, even a **low-paid** one, and stay at home.
Switch applications from design roles to workshop and maintenance jobs.
Visit the job centre, which I have avoided out of embarrassment.
feel: **Cold** and dizzy, like a bridge closing before I get across.
Guilt about my dad's bus driving into his sixties.
S2.quote: My dad is sixty and I don't want him driving buses forever because of me.
fieldNote: She is **quiet** but frightened, and she takes the pressure on her father to heart.
She uses the three-year robot delay as a thin comfort, not a plan.
Embarrassment about the job centre is **notable** and may delay her asking for help.

steps.text: Take the first workshop or maintenance job offered
Stay at dad's house to save every pound of rent
Register at the job centre this month
Write to the council and MP about graduate support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that five years is enough if people act sensibly. I'd write to the college and say they should offer proper courses in maintenance and robotics now. I'd say everyone should stay calm and plan, because panic helps nobody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's easier than two, but only just. Five years gives me time to get a first job, pay down some of the loan and move into the hands-on side. But I'd still be early in my career when thinking jobs get replaced. I'd just have a bit of a head start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get any job in a workshop and stay a few years, then see what's changing. I'd save a third of my pay and keep living at Dad's till the loan is smaller. I'd take a night course in industrial maintenance, and if it's affordable, one in programming machines, because someone must look after them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little steadier. I know that sounds odd, but a few years' warning is like having a map. It might be the wrong map, but it's something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would five years let you do that two doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not keen, honestly. I've never lived away from Dad and the town. But if the job was good and the pay covered a room, I'd go, at least for a while. I'd call Dad on Sundays and send money when I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you feel about moving away for a job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It lets me do things in order: job, then loan, then training. In two years it's all at once and I just panic. With five I can queue it up properly, and I'm good at queues.

say: I'd write to the college asking for proper **maintenance** and robotics courses now.
I'd tell everyone to stay calm and plan, because panic helps nobody.
think: Five years is easier than two, but I'd still be **early** in my career when thinking jobs go.
I'd just have a bit of a head start.
do: Get any workshop job and stay a few years, saving a **third** of my pay.
Keep living at Dad's until the loan is smaller.
Take a night course in industrial maintenance, then maybe machine programming.
feel: A little **steadier**, because a few years' warning is like having a map.
It might be the wrong map, but it's something.
S3.quote: A few years' warning is like having a map. It might be the wrong map, but it's something.
fieldNote: She values **order**: job, loan, training, in that sequence.
Moving for work is possible but unwelcome, and tied to her father.
She finds comfort in **plans**, even imperfect ones.

steps.text: Take any workshop job and stay at least two years
Save a third of every pay packet while living at home
Attend a night course in industrial maintenance
Write to the college asking for robotics maintenance courses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine and we should make sensible plans. I'd tell people not to rush into anything dramatic. Ten years is a long time and I'd want to see how things actually develop before changing my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm relieved, though not delighted. Ten years is enough for a first job, some savings and even a bit of choice. By 2039 I'd be thirty-three with a decade of experience, which has to count for something. Still, I carry the loan, and I'd be careful about promising myself anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, honestly. First job, maybe a company in maintenance or building services. Pay the loan faster than the minimum. Learn what the software does, a bit at a time, because I can't avoid it forever. Then in five or six years, look again and see if mechanical engineering is still where the jobs are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with some background worry. I'd have time to work it out, like a long walk where I can see the road ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you still pick mechanical engineering?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I think so. I like machines and I like the workshop. Ten years lets me stay with that and adjust at the edges. I like the feeling when something runs after you built it, and I wouldn't throw that away because of a headline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your dad about the loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're going to pay it, but slowly. I'd show him the numbers, because he likes numbers. I'd say in five years I'll pay for the house bills for a while, and he can finally cut his hours. That's the dream, though I wouldn't say it out loud too fast.

say: I'd tell people not to rush into anything **dramatic**.
Ten years is long enough to watch how things develop.
think: I'm relieved but not delighted, and I'd be thirty-three with a **decade** of experience.
I'd carry the loan, so I wouldn't promise myself too much.
do: Take a first job in maintenance or building services and pay the loan **faster** than the minimum.
Learn what the software does, a bit at a time.
Look again at year five or six.
feel: Like a long walk where I can see the road ahead.
S4.quote: I like the feeling when something runs after you built it, and I wouldn't throw that away because of a headline.
fieldNote: She stays steady because she **loves** the physical work of machines.
Her dream is to take over the house bills so her father can cut his hours.
Her caution is **temperamental**, not a failure of imagination.

steps.text: Take a first job in maintenance or building services
Pay the student loan faster than the minimum
Learn what workshop software does, one tool at a time
Take on the house bills so dad can cut his hours

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. It gives me no time to even get a first job, and then the thinking side of mechanical work goes straight away. What would help is simple: a proper first job scheme for graduates, loan repayments that stop if you're out of work, and someone to talk to who actually knows the industry. And the training courses that lead to real jobs, not just a certificate.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not stubborn about technology because I'm proud. I just don't like feeling pushed into things I haven't tried yet. I'd like to be given time and shown properly, like an apprentice, not told to keep up. I think a lot of people feel that and don't say it.

headlineQuote: I'm not stubborn about technology because I'm proud. I just don't like feeling pushed into things I haven't tried yet.
portrait: Olga is a **23-year-old** mechanical engineering graduate living with her bus-driver dad, with seventy applications, two interviews and no offer.
She did a gearbox test rig and a pump-factory internship, and has a good degree, **heavy** debt and almost no savings.
She is pragmatic and centrist, writes polite letters to councils, and never uses AI tools, wary of what she doesn't understand.
Her steadiness is **cautious**: she plans in order and leans on workshop, maintenance and family contacts.
She is anxious in most pictures, alarmed with two years, and uneasy only when ten years gives room to plan.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028** worries her most, because there is no time to get a first job before the thinking side goes.
whatWouldHelp: A graduate first-job **scheme**, loan repayments that stop when out of work, and training that leads to real jobs.
